transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2026-06-10 09:00 PT
Duration: ~10 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Rivera (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (CortexVault), Jon Erickson (CortexVault Eng Manager), Priya Singh (CortexVault Security)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, optional): quick sync on POC integration progress, discussed SDK callback patterns for tool/function calling, structured output validation and governance, flagged a few security questions (KMS, audit logs), agreed on next steps to run integration smoke and a Dedicated perf demo.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alyssa: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick roll call? I can see Maya and Jon and Priya, hi - thanks for making time.
[00:12] Maya: Hey, yeah thanks. We had a quick standup earlier but wanted to use this to align on the callback wiring and output schema.
[00:20] Marco: Cool. Today we'll go over the SDK approach we suggested, how function-calling works, and the structured-output validation. Also cover graceful degradation - in case the primary model is under heavy load.
[00:30] Jon: Our main ask is twofold: one, we need determinism in the JSON outputs for our parsers; two, we need predictable latency under load. We're running a mix of short chat prompts and longer transform jobs.
[00:45] Alyssa: Makes sense. For determinism we recommend the structured-output API + a small schema validator on the client. Redwood's SDK supports typed responses - the SDK can validate and optionally coerce fields. We'll share a snippet.
[01:00] Maya: When you say "coerce"—what actually happens if the model returns a string where we expect an int? Does the SDK throw or sanitize?
[01:08] Marco: Right now, the SDK has a configurable mode: strict (throws and surfaces the raw model text), and "best-effort" which attempts to coerce simple mismatches. For anything ambiguous it will attach a validation note and the original text in a metadata field.
[01:25] Priya: We need the raw also for audits, so that makes sense. Is that metadata persisted in logs? Who can access it?
[01:33] Alyssa: Metadata goes to the token-level logs in the Console. RBAC applies - only users with audit role can see full raw outputs. For Private deployments you can route logs to your SIEM and control retention via your KMS settings.
[01:46] Jon: On function calling: we prototype to call our internal "invoice-parser" tool. How do we wire callbacks so the model can request a tool and then we run it asynchronously?
[01:58] Marco: Two patterns: synchronous tool invocation and async callback flow. Synchronous is simple: model returns a tool call and the Redwood SDK will invoke the tool via a configured webhook. For async, the model emits a call token and we push the request to a queue; Redwood supports a callback URL to notify when results are available. We'll demo both.
[02:20] Maya: Any notes about retries and idempotency? We have a lot of side effects.
[02:26] Marco: Absolutely - the SDK includes idempotency keys per invocation. For async callbacks we recommend at-least-once delivery with dedup keys. Also, set max retries and backoff in the SDK config.
[02:40] Jon: Performance—we ran a small 500-request test using hosted API and saw median latency at ~120ms and p95 at 600ms, those spikes kill user experience.
[02:52] Alyssa: For those p95 spikes, two levers: batching and KV cache prefixing. If you can prefix with recent context we reduce token compute. Also Dedicated capacity gives you stable p95s - we have benchmarks we can share.
[03:10] Jon: Can you share the benchmark sheet again? The earlier link had some mismatched columns.
[03:15] Alyssa: Sure, I'll post an updated spreadsheet and a short sheet that maps our model variants to latency profiles.
[03:23] Priya: Security checklist—SOC2 scope, encryption at rest and in transit, KMS integration for Private, audit logs. We will need answers for legal.
[03:33] Alyssa: We have a security pack. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. We also provide per-request encryption metadata. I'll send the security bundle and SOC2 cert.
[03:44] Maya: A practical question on SDK: does the client side run the schema validator or do you surface a preflight endpoint from Redwood to validate sample responses?
[03:54] Marco: Both options exist. The SDK ships a local validator so you can run end-to-end checks in CI. There's also a validation endpoint you can POST a sample prompt to; Redwood will return a structured-validation result with pass/fail and example fixes.
[04:10] Jon: That validation endpoint would be useful for our CI. Any rate limits for validation? We might hammer it during testing.
[04:16] Alyssa: We'll provision a testing quota for the POC. I'll ensure you have enough tokens for CI runs during the POC window.
[04:25] Maya: About graceful degradation—what happens if the primary model variant is removed or unavailable?
[04:31] Marco: We have routing policies. Typical strategy: primary published model, then a cheaper quantized fallback. When fallback used we can add a "model_info" flag in the response so your client can adjust UX. We also have automatic fallback to a stateless response from a smaller model.
[04:50] Jon: What about hallucinations for structured fields? We need strict nulls vs fabricated values.
[04:55] Marco: Suggested pattern: use schema with explicit nullable fields and include a confidence score for each field. When confidence < threshold, the SDK sets value to null and adds an explanatory note in metadata. You can wire rules in your parser to treat metadata notes as errors.
[05:12] Priya: On retention: for hosted API we need contract-level retention windows. For Private we'll control retention. How long do logs stay by default?
[05:21] Alyssa: Default hosted retention is 90 days for full logs, with token-level retention configurable at the account level. We can add longer retention as an add-on.
[05:33] Maya: A few edge cases we hit: 1) tool invocation that returns non-JSON payloads; 2) model calling the wrong tool name due to name confusion; 3) nested structured outputs where arrays sometimes are strings.
[05:45] Marco: For (1) we recommend a content-type enforcement layer on the webhook; the SDK can reject non-JSON responses. For (2) namespace your tools (e.g., invoice.parse.v1) to reduce collisions. For (3) the validator will coerce and emit validation errors for arrays that are strings, you can fail the job in CI or coerce.
[06:10] Jon: Any examples of how to name tools? We have many microservices.
[06:16] Marco: Use dot-separated namespaces and semantic versions. Example: com.cortexvault.invoice.parser.v1. Also include capability tags so model can reason about tool intent.
[06:30] Maya: Quick note—our legal team will need the export controls and data residency documentation for EU users.
[06:37] Alyssa: Noted, will include residency docs. We have region pins for EU and APAC.
[06:43] Priya: On auditability—if a user triggers a tool call that results in an external side effect, we need the full chain of events. Can Redwood surface a single trace ID?
[06:51] Marco: Yes, we generate a request trace id that ties model prompt, model response, tool call, and callback. That can also be forwarded to your tracing system.
[07:05] Jon: Ok, about the demo: we want Redwood to set up a Dedicated demo with a load pattern approximating 200 RPS for 30 minutes—this will show p95 under sustained load.
[07:16] Marco: We can do that on our Dedicated demo cluster. We'll need an agreement on test datasets and cost estimate. I'll prepare a config and cost sheet.
[07:25] Maya: For the POC acceptance criteria: 1) structured output pass rate >= 98% for schema checks; 2) p95 latency < 400ms for chat flows; 3) secure logs with RBAC - legal sign-off. Does that align?
[07:37] Alyssa: Yes, that seems reasonable. We'll work toward those targets. For the schema pass rate we'll instrument the validator and report daily.
[07:46] Jon: Small nit—some of our parsers want deterministic IDs generated by the model. Is there support for deterministic seeding?
[07:55] Marco: We have a deterministic sampling mode for some model families, and we can also offer post-processing to derive stable IDs from content.
[08:10] Maya: Anything else on function calling? We saw some earlier tests where the model produced a tool name with small typos.
[08:18] Marco: That's why we recommend a strict tool name set and a pre-deployment run where we test common prompts. The validation endpoint can catch those.
[08:30] Priya: For security review—I'll send a list of required controls: encryption keys rotation, SSO/SAML, minimum account separation, audit export. Can Redwood respond within 3 business days?
[08:41] Alyssa: Yes, once you email the list we'll prioritize. I'll loop in our security engineer.
[08:50] Maya: Let's recap next steps.
[08:53] Alyssa: Recap: 1) Alyssa will share SDK snippet for callback wiring and validation endpoint link; 2) Jon to run smoke and post lat/dist; 3) Marco prepare Dedicated demo config and cost; 4) Priya to send security questions; 5) Redwood to provision test quota. Any other items?
[09:12] Jon: I'll also share a small corpus of 500 invoices for the validation runs.
[09:18] Alyssa: Great. We'll have a follow-up next week same time to review smoke results.
[09:22] Maya: Thanks everyone.
[09:24] Priya: Thanks.
[09:25] Alyssa: Thanks, bye.
